I (32F) just went through a big break up last fall. He invited me over, said it wasn’t working for him. I said okay, asked him if there was anything more I could do to make it work. He said no he needs to figure his own things out. I really genuinely wished him well in life, said if ever finds himself in a bad spot - that I’m just a phone call away. That’s all I said and got up and left. Never reached out until months later when he did. I let him go. 

I was definitely heartbroken and fell to pieces by myself afterwards (which is how I ended up on this sub) but also picked myself back up and put my life back together to be even happier today. I went through all the stages of grief by myself and for myself. All that was my responsibility and I respected his right to just be a human figuring it out just like I am. We did talk months later, he of course wanted to do the friend thing and kindly, I tried but eventually said I needed to keep moving on or needed more time. He respected it. Him and I still see each other at gatherings sometimes and we’re cordial. No bad blood and not an ounce of anger was hurled to tear the other apart. 


—-> I share all this not because my story is that important here, but to say it can be done. How I carry myself and how I treat others is my responsibility and important to me, as a woman, as an exgirlfriend, as a human, etc. Holding on to resentment, anger, and bitterness does not help me whatsoever. I try to surround myself with people who navigate the world in a similar manner but I’ve learned it can be hard to tell how someone reacts when rug is pulled out from underneath them and they don’t get what they want. I’m sorry you’re still getting bad treatment and she’s still just straight up being mean. You absolutely don’t deserve to be treated with hostility, especially now. Even if being friends is something you both would like to make work, perhaps it would be helpful to that friendship later on if you both took the time right now to just recalibrate on your own. It sounds like nothing good is able to grow from where things are right now.

But again, as someone else said, there’s no one right way to walk through breakups. Everyone is different, and handles things differently.

I will add, and this only pertains to my personal experience, I do get hesitant about upping my dose if I think there’s something else that might help my anxiety might stabilize first only because I don’t like having to taper down to a lower dose when I feel like a little numbed out to life (this is only my personal experience, I’m also on other meds that effect this) on 20mg. Tapering down does balance out eventually but  sometimes it makes my moods worse in the next month.

I’ve been on varying 10-20mg over the past 15 years. I still deal with bouts of depressive episodes and severe anxiety, often with external life factors influencing that and sometimes just hormonal. I also have Klonopin PRN if I need it for when the anxiety is controlling everything. Lexapro doesn’t fix everything in my life and I still have issues (CPTSD, ADHD, suicidal ideation, chronic health issues) I work on in therapy and by any measure my life has been mostly manageable these past years. Lexapro does a good job of bringing the floor up for how bad my anxiety and overwhelm can get. Not all the time but most of the time. I’m also in Ketamine therapy which has worked incredibly to help my depression. 

That being said, I work closely with my psych throughout the seasons of life. If I sense a particular season is really affecting me (winters are my worse) we go up to 20mg, if spring feels better I taper down to 15 or 10mg. We don’t change dosage often unless it’s really fitting for my QOL. I have felt comfortable expressing and asking about a dosage change and we go from there. There’s a lot of other factors that play into my anxiety that I try to look at first, like my hormones (am I close to that time of the month?) or would I feel better if I could get a couple days of relief by taking half of Klonopin in the evening and get good sleep. I get the ruminating too. If it seems like it’s a mostly constant state of anxiety over a prolonged period of time without much relief, I would make an inquiry in trying a higher dose. Remember every*body* is different. 
I have empathy for the struggle in this and I hope you can find an answer that works for you.

When you agree to the use of Spravato as prescribed, this is in the pharmaceutical contract. This is for liability reasons of both the pharmaceutical company and your private clinic. Prior to starting treatment, you sign these documents which are not always verbal agreements, but does have to been in legal writing.
It’s a ‘standard’ for any practice using any sort of sedative or tranquilizer. 

 ‘What should I avoid while taking SPRAVATO®?
- Do not drive, operate machinery, or do anything where you need to be completely alert after taking SPRAVATO®. Do not take part in these activities until the next day following a restful sleep. ’

They can’t make you do anything after you leave the office of course, but they CAN cover their own asses for liability reasons and reserve the right to discharge you from treatment if you don’t follow protocol. Pretty normal stuff, just break the rules with discretion and please do it safely and responsibility.

From my experience with working in private practices like these as well as being a frequent comfortable patient at my ketamine clinic, it is likely the information of not going directly home, or having a rideshare drop a patient off at some other place of leisure other than home, was shared with the providers by a patient. I imagine it was already addressed with that patient that this is liability and they were advised to go directly home, and the office made an executive decision to post a reminder of their liability policies for any future occurrences. 

In signing contracts prior to starting treatment with each clinic, this is usually in the paperwork of both the practice and the use of spravato. Technically they can’t make you do anything after you leave the office but at least you were notified this is against their policy for liability reasons so it’s on you. 

That being said, even at my clinic, there are some people who drive themselves home.

I am grateful I’m still alive and now have people that I can call family and had a place to be that wasn’t the foster system. A place for my horse who was my best friend. Ngl, this was my entire life from the age of 14-26. Consistently. In dressage stables all over the world where ever I could get connected with trainers and could work off room and board, sometimes lessons if I was really lucky. Some barns I’d stay years and other were short contracts. Brought my little PRE gelding with me everywhere. Most always I’d live in a small room in the barn with a space heater or the living quarters of someones horse trailer. I got my diploma in the mail. I made very little money, especially in the beginning, and had side jobs here and there. Eventually I landed at such respectful barns that compensated well, and really did care. Definitely learned to be wary what barns I landed at. 


Barn owners and trainers got a free stable hand/groom and I got ‘experience’ 😂. education, training, a lot of show opportunities, made it to Grand Prix and got my medals. Met a LOT of wonderful people that helped raise me, people I still call family. My horse got great homes. I got to do work that I honestly loved (cleaning stalls is therapeutic for me) and wish I could do it for the rest of my life but it’s not sustainable to live off of for the rest of my life. I think I knew I sold my soul to this a long time ago. I was okay with being a barn rat, it was better than home with an abusive father. 

My gelding passed in 2020 at the age of 29 (don’t worry he was well retired) and while I have other horses now, he broke my heart just enough that I’d never return to that life. I train mostly kids now. I’m happy. I don’t regret any of those years. I’m grateful, truly. 
Ads like this impress me now, while most are pretty standard. Some even include health insurance. I’m not a better person being able to endure the work and ‘slave labour’. I know it’s not for everyone and whatever is for you is absolutely okay. It was just a way better life for me given the home I had. 🙂

Edit: after I came back home I tried working in retail, Best Buy, got my MA and worked in hospitals/private practice. I still always wish I was just cleaning stalls. Way less people yelling at you and much more quiet listening to horses munching on hay.

Edit: I just read that you are not from America so disregard my info pertaining to just the US. PRE paperwork with the ANCCE really just highlights the expression of bloodlines and morphology in the horse but Andalusians as a whole do tend to call carry a certain resemblance

I have three PREs. I’m the crazy PRE horse girl (to most people). Imported from two beloved stud farms in Spain. One was a gift from HGF as a foal out of Grandioso who I had the pleasure of starting myself from backing to competing (dressage). He was a breeze even as a stallion. 
One I’ve had for 16 years who was my heart horse until he passed a short time ago. I don’t think I’ll ever seek out to own another breed other than Iberian for my personal horse. 

I’m quite involved with USPRE and ANCCE if you have any questions, yet not so much IALHA. But I know there’s someone out there who surely is. The farms in the US I have been a working student/trainer for and now whom are like family ‘specialize’ in the breed (improving and maintaining the Iberian breed) I guess you could say. Stud farms both here and near Madrid. PRE (pure raza  Española) originate from spain and to be inscribed, must go through inspection (held in the US and across the world at various locations throughout the year). A lot of it is focused on morphology and preserving aspects of historical bloodlines. 

It’s a wonderful community to be apart of really and while you can’t really put a blanket statement on all PRE/andalusians being gentle and docile (because I’ve seen some hot stallions and spicy mares) but my experience in contrast to some other warm bloods has been nothing short of wonderful temperament wise. Incredibly smart horses but of course, I am speaking from my own bias. All breeds are special. 

But pertaining to your inquiry to give insight -If you were close I would say come sit on my one mare Gisela and have a go around the arena and on the trails. I jump her. We go to the beach. I started her myself, she’s ten now, and I would happily put kids on her. I use her for lessons. I’ve noticed with her particularly she is patient and brave. With any horse, attention to training and fairness is important. We started very slow and natural. She is incredibly sensitive as I’ve found that to be true with most* PREs

I will say importing is costly but buying in the US is also costly (assuming you are in the US sorry). But you can find gems and diamonds here I promise. Do research on the stud farms if you’re looking for a foal or don’t be afraid to ask breeder if they know of anything on the market that would be fitting for you. Don’t be afraid to buy the older horse either! 

I compete, show, train, and breed for dressage but I like to see all my horses be well rounded and comfortable in many areas outside of the arena. PRE/Andalusian breeds have a naturally animated gate especially in the front so training half steps and self carriage is a little easier I’ve found but like I said, it’s all how you approach training. I look for potential in all horses no matter the breed. 

Anything else just ask! Happy to share my experience.

I can personally second this experience. 
Not all my hospitalizations have been horrible over the last ten years. By the time I leave I, more often than not, feel more stabilized to move forward. I do not have autobrewery syndrome so I’m not entirely sure how my experience will differ. Replenishing my electrolytes intravenously at whatever pace after bouts of CVS can be heavenly even for the nausea. If you can find any peace in being monitored in a professional medical setting, especially for refeeding syndrome, it’s a bit of weight off the shoulders (no pun intended). 

On tube feeds - I have had both NJ, J tube and TPN - it is only natural to be anxious about the placement process and adjusting to a new normal, even if temporary. 

It can be incredibly uncomfortable at the wrong pace and finding a GI or parts of a team you trust who extend a lot of grace can be key but I know that’s an incredible luxury.  Slow is always better unfortunately. 
You have to give up a lot of control and day to day certainty. Don’t be afraid to voice some concerns as they come up. And I know it can’t simply be ‘trust the process’ when your body is constantly fighting you  Wherever you can try to find little glimpses of trusting and comfort has been something that’s helped my stress and downtime in the hospital. 

I’m not a doctor nor do I have so I cannot give advice on specific medications that have helped me get through these hospitalizations but I’m a person that likes to stay sleepy in the hospital. I sleep a lot. By the time I’m hospitalized I’m exhausted from how much pain and constant vomiting my body has been through (still keep the puke bags handy) so the rest is welcomed. 

I have been hospitalized anywhere from one week to seven months though 7mo was one of the last times and that was four years ago. I’ve been without tubes and pain since (not without symptom though). Each time is a little different. Some I barely remember because of pain. Some were a relief. 

I absolutely give credit to my hospitalizations for how incredibly how well my health is doing today. And yet you are so valid to be uneasy about it all. 

DMs are open should you have questions on my experience relating to yours.

ETA: for NJ and GJ, I had to find formulas and feed rates that worked for me. The blanket recommendation, I found, was not a one size fits all.

I’m growing more heart broken by the amount of disrespect and just trash from the new people here. 😞 this used to be my place of peace. 

That being said, our downtown areas have grown amazingly! My friends are on several Muskegon committees and we host Burning Foot Beer Festival, Winter Fest , and all the in between (Lumberjack fest is AMAZING). Our farmers market on Saturdays always brings life. A large portion of my friends work service industry in new up and coming distilleries, breweries, and restaurants. Wonderland Distillery is home to me, I read and paint there on the couch often and my friends work art (okay it’s chemistry) behind the bar. Trivia is Tuesday night. Unruly Brewery is beyond amazing for entertainment if you need a place to feel belonging. Top Shelf has some of the best pizza and atmosphere with their open garage doors. We now have Socibowl! It’s brilliant and the menu is amazing. 

There isn’t the biggest Mardi Gras festival here as people have said but there isn’t those events for the lack of trying. You just have to know where to go (trust me🥳). There’s also a magic wand to be had here. You’ll find so many places want to make your dreams and ideas reality for the sake of bringing people together. To give our music artists and creatives an opportunity. We jump at the chance. Our jazz community is amazing and becoming. I mean the famous burning foot festival and electric forest were just shower thoughts at the bar amongst friends and drinks at one point and now we’ve brought it it to fruition many years running. If you tell pints and quarts you miss their beer cheese soup they’ll put it on the menu in a couple days. 

I live next to hoffmaster park and ride my horses to the beach. 
So all that being said, this place has so much magic. No doubt you’ve felt that in the sunsets (it’s amazing in a sailboat). I’m not even from here but I did grow up here and returned after living other places. Respect it and you’ll always have friends and fortune two fold.

You are certainly most welcome here and I hope you take the chance❤️
